title: Vectors, matrices, and frames: when mathematics becomes a robot action

blocks.text: This chapter starts with an assembly problem rather than the definition of matrix multiplication. A camera observes a datum point on an aero-engine blade, and the robot must turn that observation into a target pose in the base frame. A matrix is therefore an action with an input space, an output space, units, and physical meaning; multiplication composes actions. We finish with a runnable NumPy laboratory and a frame-aware class that prevents the most dangerous coordinate bugs.

blocks.text: 2.0 Where matrices come from: collecting many operations into one action

Do not begin by treating a matrix as a table of numbers. Suppose an assembly table maps $(x,y)$ to two outputs. If the rules are $u=2x-y$ and $v=x+3y$, collect the coefficients according to which output depends on which input.

blocks.text: A matrix is not an arbitrary notation: it compresses a collection of linear equations into a reusable input-output interface. A $2\times2$ matrix means two inputs and two outputs. If the input has three entries while the output still has two, the matrix naturally becomes $2\times3$.

blocks.title: 先问三个问题，再做矩阵乘法 / Ask three questions before multiplying

blocks.text: What is the input object? What are the units and frame of each component? What is the output object? Multiplication has physical meaning only when input space, output space, and units match.
2.1 Start from the task: turning a camera point into a robot action

Suppose a camera observes a datum hole on an aero-engine blade. The vision module returns image coordinates $(u,v)$, a depth module reconstructs a point $p^C$ in the camera frame, and the controller needs the same point $p^B$ in the robot-base frame. For a camera fixed on the workbench, the minimal computational chain is

The equation is short, but it hides four engineering questions. Are the coordinates in metres or millimetres? Does the subscript $BC$ mean “express $C$ in $B$” under our convention? Should a point and a free direction vector use the same transform? How large can calibration error be before the assembly clearance is exhausted? Each hidden question becomes an explicit interface or check in this chapter.

blocks.text: 2.2 A vector is not merely a column of numbers: semantics, units, and frames first

A vector is first a semantic object and only then a sequence of numbers. A position says where a point is, a displacement says how one position changes to another, a velocity says how position changes over time, and an error says how the current state differs from a target. They may all have three entries, but equal shapes do not make them interchangeable.

The superscript $B$ denotes a coordinate frame; subscripts can denote an object or a time role. A reliable engineering record must answer what an array represents, in which frame, in which unit, and at which timestamp. Such metadata are often omitted on paper; in a real robot, that omission is a source of failure.

blocks.text: An immediate check

When you see `error = goal - current`, do not first ask whether NumPy can execute it. Ask whether the arrays represent the same kind of object, share a frame, share a unit, and refer to compatible times. Only four “yes” answers make the subtraction physically meaningful.
2.3 Matrix order: a contract between input and output spaces

Let $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be an $n$-dimensional column vector and $y\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ an $m$-dimensional output. A matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ represents a linear map from the input space to the output space: $y=Ax$. Thus, $m$ rows and $n$ columns are not formatting facts; they state how many input components the action consumes and how many output components it produces.
From the row view, each row is a linear measurement of the input. From the column view, column $j$ is the image of the input basis vector $e_j$. Therefore

The columns tell us what happens to the basis directions of the input space. For a rotation matrix, columns are the rotated coordinate axes; for a camera projection, they describe image changes caused by 3-D directions. The later Jacobian will reuse this interpretation, but this chapter does not require computing one yet.

2.4 Why matrix multiplication has an order: composition of actions
If action $A$ first maps an input to an intermediate object $z$ and action $B$ maps $z$ to the output $y$, then
The rightmost matrix acts first because this is function composition. If a point goes from the tool frame $E$ to the wrist frame $W$ and then to the base frame $B$, the chain is

Swapping two matrices often does not trigger a shape error because the dimensions remain compatible, but it changes the physical action. The following planar example deliberately separates “translate then rotate” from “rotate then translate.”

Both results look like reasonable coordinates, but they describe different actions. In research code, a transform chain should be expressed by frame labels and tests rather than by the author's memory.
2.5 Rotation matrices: preserving length and angle, not arbitrary 2-D matrices
A 2-D rotation matrix is determined by one angle:
It satisfies $R^TR=I$ and $\det R=1$. The first identity says the columns are orthonormal; the second excludes a mirror reflection. Therefore

This derivation explains why rotation does not change the distance between two points on a rigid body. It also gives a code assertion: if a purported rotation changes lengths noticeably, first check angle units, numeric types, and frame indices before tuning a controller.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

def rotate_90(vector: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    vector = np.asarray(vector, dtype=float)
    if vector.shape != (2,):
        raise ValueError("expected a two-dimensional vector")
    rotation = np.array([[0.0, -1.0],
                         [1.0,  0.0]])
    result = rotation @ vector
    assert np.isclose(np.linalg.norm(result), np.linalg.norm(vector))
    assert np.allclose(rotation.T @ rotation, np.eye(2))
    return result

point_local = np.array([1.0, 2.0])
print(rotate_90(point_local))  # [-2.  1.]

blocks.text: 2.6 Frames: several numerical expressions of one physical point

A physical point has one location, but its numerical expression can differ across frames. A camera observes $p^C$, the robot base uses $p^B$, and a world model uses $p^W$. Frame labels must be explicit; otherwise subtraction, interpolation, and control errors have no precise meaning.

blocks.caption: 一个物理点的多 frame 表达，以及 frame 误差如何消耗装配间隙 / One physical point in multiple frames, and how frame error consumes assembly clearance

blocks.text: Do not casually mix active rotation of an object with passive change of coordinates. A project may choose either convention, but it must fix the convention and state input and output frames in every API.
二维图上的 $R(\theta)$ 只有一个角度；三维刚体位姿属于 $SE(3)$，旋转有三个自由度，常用 $3\times3$ 旋转矩阵与三维平移组合成 $4\times4$ 齐次变换。这里暂时不要求你先学习 Lie 群；你只需记住两个不变的工程问题：每个矩阵描述哪两个 frame，以及它作用在点、向量还是速度上。后续第 27 章再建立 $SO(3)$、$SE(3)$ 和指数映射的完整桥接。
2.7 Homogeneous transforms: why append a 1

Rotation is written as $Rp$ and translation as $p+t$. With only a $2\times2$ matrix, translation cannot be composed by the same multiplication. Homogeneous coordinates augment a planar point to $\tilde p=[p^T,1]^T$:

Expanding the last row shows that the homogeneous component remains one; expanding the first two rows gives $p^B=R_{BA}p^A+t_{BA}$. The extra dimension does not add a physical degree of freedom. It embeds an affine action in a composable linear representation.

The difference between a point and a direction vector is explicit in homogeneous coordinates: a point has last component 1, while a free vector has last component 0. The same $T$ therefore translates a point but not a direction.
2.8 Transform chains: use subscripts as a type system
Use the convention that $T_{BA}$ converts an expression in frame $A$ into an expression in frame $B$. Then

blocks.latex:
T_{BA}:A\to B,\qquad T_{CB}:B\to C,\qquad
  T_{CA}=T_{CB}T_{BA}:A\to C.

blocks.text: This is analogous to function types or unit checking: a chain is legal only when the output frame of one transform equals the input frame of the next. Bare matrices allow many dimensionally valid but physically wrong products; frame-aware objects can reject them early.

blocks.text: 2.9 Runnable lab I: a FrameTransform that fails loudly

The class below stores four pieces of metadata together: source frame, target frame, length unit, and matrix. It is not object-oriented ornamentation; it turns a physical constraint that would otherwise live only in comments into an executable check.

Inspect the interface before inspecting the numbers. The last homogeneous component is 1 for `apply_point` and effectively 0 for `apply_vector`; `then` allows $A\to B$ only to be followed by $B\to C$. These design choices determine whether later numerical results deserve trust.

blocks.code:
transform = FrameTransform.from_angle_translation(
    source="camera", target="base", unit="m",
    theta_rad=np.deg2rad(90.0), translation=[2.0, 3.0]
)
point_base = transform.apply_point([1.0, 0.0])
vector_base = transform.apply_vector([1.0, 0.0])
assert np.allclose(point_base, [2.0, 4.0])
assert np.allclose(vector_base, [0.0, 1.0])

blocks.text: If a free direction is incorrectly passed as a point, the result is $[2,4]^T$ instead of $[0,1]^T$. This can simultaneously corrupt end-effector orientation, contact normals, and force-control directions without raising an exception.
2.10 Runnable lab II: planar calibration from corresponding rigid points

We now move from a known matrix action to an action estimated from data. Camera-to-base extrinsics can be estimated from corresponding points. Given camera points $p_i^C$ and base points $p_i^B$, we seek
Translation and rotation are coupled in the original expression. Subtracting the two centroids removes translation:

Let $H=(Q^C)^TQ^B$ and compute its SVD $H=U\Sigma V^T$. The 2-D Kabsch solution is $R=VDU^T$, with the last singular direction negated if the unconstrained solution is a reflection. This estimates a matrix while preserving the rigid-body constraint instead of fitting unconstrained entries.

blocks.code:
source_center = source.mean(axis=0)
target_center = target.mean(axis=0)
centered_source = source - source_center
centered_target = target - target_center
covariance = centered_source.T @ centered_target
u, singular_values, vt = np.linalg.svd(covariance)
correction = np.eye(2)
if np.linalg.det(vt.T @ u.T) < 0.0:
    correction[-1, -1] = -1.0
r = vt.T @ correction @ u.T
t = target_center - r @ source_center

blocks.text: The smallest singular value also supports degeneracy detection. If all calibration points nearly coincide, or their geometry is insufficient to determine rotation, the SVD tells us that the problem is unidentifiable instead of returning a seemingly precise pose.
2.11 Error, noise, and conditioning: why point layout matters

Even without obvious outliers, a point set may be unable to estimate rotation stably. If points are tightly clustered, small pixel or depth noise can cause a large angular change; if they are nearly collinear, information in some directions is missing. Numerical linear algebra describes this as ill-conditioning or a large condition number.

Here $\kappa$ is not an abstract score of algorithm quality; it warns how the data geometry amplifies error. A calibration experiment should report point-set scale, spatial coverage, the smallest singular value, fit RMSE, and repetitions across noise levels and seeds rather than one attractive matrix.
若叶片装配允许的平面位置误差只有 $0.20\,\mathrm{mm}$，而标定的平移 RMSE 已为 $0.35\,\mathrm{mm}$，继续训练策略网络并不能修复这个几何瓶颈。应先检查相机内参、外参、点的空间覆盖和单位约定。只有几何误差低于任务容差，后续的规划和强化学习才有机会学习到真正的装配策略。
2.12 Shapes, units, and assertions in code

A NumPy array knows its shape and dtype, but not metres, base frame, or whether it is a direction. The minimum coding standard in this book is therefore not “it runs” but “errors become visible early.”

blocks.text: For example, `np.matmul` can multiply a $(3,3)$ matrix by a $(3,)$ array, but it cannot tell whether that array is a point or a vector, nor which way the matrix maps frames. A good interface preserves semantics before and after the call; a good experiment gives a diagnostic message when an assertion fails.
2.13 Full experiment: from ground truth and noise to a reproducible report

Running `linear_algebra_frames_lab.py` produces four metrics: fit RMSE, the ground-truth RMSE on noisy data, translation error, and rotation error. A fixed seed makes the run reproducible; it does not make one seed sufficient evidence for a method.

blocks.code:
def run_calibration_demo(seed: int = 7, noise_std: float = 0.002):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    source = np.array([[0.0, 0.0], [0.30, 0.02],
                       [0.06, 0.25], [0.22, 0.31]])
    truth = FrameTransform.from_angle_translation(
        "camera", "base", "m", np.deg2rad(27.0), [0.42, -0.18])
    target_clean = np.vstack([truth.apply_point(p) for p in source])
    target_noisy = target_clean + rng.normal(
        0.0, noise_std, size=target_clean.shape)
    estimate = fit_rigid_2d(source, target_noisy, unit="m")
    return calibration_rmse(estimate, source, target_noisy)

In research, changing one variable at a time is more valuable than running arbitrary extra trials. First fix the point set and ground truth and sweep noise; then fix noise and compare clustered points with points covering the workspace. This separates algorithmic error from observation geometry.
2.13A Complete source and contract tests: matrices must carry frame semantics

The hand calculations and snippets above explain how a matrix acts. The complete module below explains how software rejects physically meaningless but dimensionally legal multiplication. `FrameTransform` stores source, target, unit, and a homogeneous matrix. Points use homogeneous coordinate 1, vectors use only the rotation block, composition requires matching intermediate frames and units, and inversion swaps semantic direction. A bare matrix lacks this information and should remain an internal implementation rather than a system interface.

blocks.text: Tests first distinguish translation semantics for points and vectors, then check frame composition and unit mismatch. They recover a ground-truth transform from noiseless correspondences, perform an inverse round trip, inject a NaN angle, a non-orthogonal rotation, collinear calibration points, and empty RMSE data, and finally verify exact report reproducibility under a fixed seed. If foundational geometry fails, PnP, hand--eye calibration, visual servoing, and multi-robot state fusion must not continue.

import unittest

import numpy as np

from linear_algebra_frames_lab import (
    FrameError,
    FrameTransform,
    calibration_rmse,
    fit_rigid_2d,
    rotation,
    run_calibration_demo,
)


class LinearAlgebraFramesTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_point_and_vector_have_different_translation_semantics(self) -> None:
        transform = FrameTransform.from_angle_translation("A", "B", "m", np.pi / 2, [2.0, 3.0])
        np.testing.assert_allclose(transform.apply_point([1.0, 0.0]), [2.0, 4.0])
        np.testing.assert_allclose(transform.apply_vector([1.0, 0.0]), [0.0, 1.0], atol=1e-12)


    def test_composition_checks_intermediate_frame(self) -> None:
        first = FrameTransform.from_angle_translation("A", "B", "m", 0.0, [1.0, 0.0])
        second = FrameTransform.from_angle_translation("B", "C", "m", 0.0, [0.0, 2.0])
        composed = first.then(second)
        np.testing.assert_allclose(composed.apply_point([0.0, 0.0]), [1.0, 2.0])
        with self.assertRaises(FrameError):
            first.then(FrameTransform.from_angle_translation("C", "D", "m", 0.0, [0.0, 0.0]))


    def test_svd_rigid_fit_recovers_transform_with_small_noise(self) -> None:
        source = np.array([[0.0, 0.0], [0.3, 0.0], [0.0, 0.2], [0.2, 0.3]])
        truth = FrameTransform.from_angle_translation("source", "target", "m", 0.35, [0.4, -0.1])
        target = np.vstack([truth.apply_point(point) for point in source])
        estimate = fit_rigid_2d(source, target)
        np.testing.assert_allclose(estimate.matrix, truth.matrix, atol=1e-10)

    def test_inverse_round_trip_and_unit_mismatch(self) -> None:
        transform = FrameTransform.from_angle_translation("camera", "base", "m", .4, [.2, -.1])
        point = np.array([.3, .5])
        np.testing.assert_allclose(transform.inverse().apply_point(transform.apply_point(point)), point)
        with self.assertRaises(FrameError):
            transform.then(FrameTransform.from_angle_translation("base", "tool", "mm", 0., [0., 0.]))

    def test_invalid_rigid_geometry_fails_at_admission(self) -> None:
        with self.assertRaises(FrameError):
            rotation(np.nan)
        with self.assertRaises(FrameError):
            FrameTransform("A", "B", "m", [[2., 0., 0.], [0., 1., 0.], [0., 0., 1.]])
        with self.assertRaises(FrameError):
            fit_rigid_2d([[0., 0.], [1., 0.], [2., 0.]], [[0., 0.], [1., 0.], [2., 0.]])
        with self.assertRaises(FrameError):
            calibration_rmse(FrameTransform.from_angle_translation("A", "B", "m", 0., [0., 0.]), [], [])

    def test_calibration_demo_is_deterministic(self) -> None:
        self.assertEqual(run_calibration_demo(seed=11), run_calibration_demo(seed=11))
        with self.assertRaises(FrameError):
            run_calibration_demo(noise_std=-1.)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

blocks.title: From the planar teaching baseline to 3-D $SE(3)$

blocks.text: When moving to $4\times4$ transforms, retain source, target, and unit; replace the $SO(2)$ check with $SO(3)$; keep homogeneous coordinates 1/0 for points/vectors; preserve frame rules for composition and inversion; and generalize planar collinearity to insufficient 3-D point or motion excitation. Keep these test semantics before replacing implementation with Lie groups, quaternions, or a robotics library.
2.14 Failure cases: why a plausible result can still be wrong
Failure 1: mixing degrees and radians

Python trigonometric functions use radians. If $90$ is passed as radians, $\cos(90)$ is about $-0.448$, not 0. The matrix remains $2\times2$ and the program runs; only invariants or visualization reveal the error.
Failure 2: using the inverse instead of the forward transform

Extrinsic files often use names such as camera-to-base and base-to-camera. If one reads only “extrinsics” and does not test a known point, $T_{BC}$ and $T_{CB}=T_{BC}^{-1}$ are easily swapped. A minimal test maps a known point to the camera and back and checks the error against a tolerance.
Failure 3: transforming a normal as a point

A contact normal should be affected only by rotation. If a normal starts at $[0,1]^T$, an incorrect point transform adds translation and produces a vector with wrong length and direction. The code should expose separate `apply_point` and `apply_vector` methods instead of one “universal transform.”
Failure 4: sending millimetres into a metre-based simulator

If vision outputs $[120,80]$ mm but the simulator receives $[120,80]$ m, the target lies hundreds of times outside the workspace. A subtler case converts units in only one module, leaving half the chain in mm and half in m. Normalize units at system boundaries and record them in data structures and logs.
2.15 From matrices to the rest of robotics
The matrices in this chapter are not an isolated mathematics island. They reappear throughout the rest of the book:

items: Jacobian: each column is a joint-velocity contribution to end-effector velocity; its shape follows the degrees of freedom and task space.
Vision: intrinsics and extrinsics connect pixels, camera points, and base points; projection dimensions express the 3-D to 2-D compression.
Control: define the error in one frame, and match the gain matrix to input and output units.
Planning: a discretized trajectory becomes a state matrix, and constraints become linear inequalities or local linearizations.
Calibration and estimation: least squares, QR, SVD, and conditioning determine whether geometry is identifiable.
Multi-robot coordination: transform local states and constraints into a shared world or task frame before communication.

选择一个旋转和一个非零平移，$R T$ 与 $T R$ 的平移部分不同。
正交性给出 $R^TR=I$，角度加法给出逆旋转为负角度。
$T=\begin{bmatrix}\cos30^\circ&-\sin30^\circ&0.2\\\sin30^\circ&\cos30^\circ&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}$，前提是平移在输出 frame 中定义。
取一个非原点点，分别用 $T$ 和 $T^{-1}$ 变换，并与已知物理位置比较。
齐次分量决定是否包含平移：点为 1，方向为 0。
非共线点提供不同方向的信息；集中或近共线会让协方差矩阵接近秩亏。
至少需要单位、点数和布局、噪声模型、随机种子、重复次数、置信区间、容差和是否在真实传感器条件下测得。

blocks.title: Oral template: why does matrix multiplication have an order?

blocks.text: I do not explain matrix multiplication as a rule to memorize. If $A$ maps an input to an intermediate space and $B$ maps the intermediate space to the output, the composition is $B(Ax)=(BA)x$. In robotics, the frame subscripts must also match, so $T_{CB}T_{BA}$ means $A$ to $B$ followed by $B$ to $C$. Swapping the order may remain dimensionally valid but changes the physical action.

blocks.text: 本章达到最低完成标准的证据是：

items: 不看笔记手算一个二维变换链，并能解释每个下标；
运行代码，故意交换两个 frame，看到异常而不是得到静默错误；
用四个对应点拟合刚体变换，报告 RMSE、平移误差、旋转误差和 seed；
构造一个退化点集，解释为什么不能相信拟合结果；
用中文和英文各口述一次“点、向量、矩阵乘法和齐次变换”的关系；
写出一个能被后续运动学或装配代码复用的接口，而不是只在 notebook 中打印数组；
运行本章代码测试，解释矩阵形状、单位、frame 和一个故意触发的退化案例。

blocks.text: 如果这些证据还没有完成，本章不是“忘记了”，而是尚未学完；回到相应小节做最小实验即可。
本章出口：用带版本、单位、frame 和 seed 的标定代码，报告拟合 RMSE、退化指标和可视化；再把最大位置误差与叶片容差比较，决定优先改进视觉、标定、规划还是控制。
